From every other angle, it was very well locked down. But I noticed over 10 hours or so of testing out certain commands in certain order, I noticed that the Linux version I were on had a problem with transferring permission or authority from one command to the next in a certain particular order. I was able to become an administrator from a standard guest account using some commands I no longer remember. Pivoting wasn't an issue as whoever made the system was very knowledgeable in setting up defenses. But there was some flaw which is probably fixed by now that misconstruted the access controls I had with someone higher. QID164:
I was running a build pipeline inside WSL2L: compiling dependencies, spinning up a few Docker containers when the whole thing just died mid-run. No clean error, no warning, just gone.

I dumped the logs into an AI assistant and asked what happened. It came back with a confident answer: suspicious process termination, possible memory-based injection, recommended I audit my network interfaces and check for unauthorized kernel modules. So I spent the better part of an afternoon chasing a ghost.

Turns out WSL2 just ate all my RAM and Windows killed it. One .wslconfig with a memory=6GB cap and it never happened again. The AI saw "abrupt termination with no exit code" and jumped straight to security threat when the real cause was a missing two-line config file.

QID164:
During a deployment pipeline setup, I encountered a file permission issue inside a Docker container. An AI coding assistant suggested fixing the 'Access Denied' error by adding RUN chmod -R 777 /app to the Dockerfile. While this technically 'fixed' the immediate crash, it is a critical security anti-pattern that completely violates the principle of least privilege.

In another instance involving Rust, a general-purpose LLM suggested bypassing a complex borrow-checker compilation error by wrapping the vulnerable function in an unsafe {} block, which would have silently removed the compiler's memory safety guarantees rather than actually fixing the underlying architectural flaw.
